editorial.body: (사설) 형사소송법 개정안이 국회 본회의에 상정되어 검찰 보완수사권 미부여 등 논란이 일고 있다. 범죄 피해자 보호, 공소기각 사유 확대 등 형사사법제도 변화로 국민적 우려가 커지고 있다. |
summary: 형사소송법 개정안이 국회 본회의에 상정돼 검찰 보완수사권 논란이 일고 있다.

editorial.titleTr: Prosecution Under Fire, President Protected: Rushed and Contradictory Criminal Procedure Law
summaryTr: An amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act has been submitted to the National Assembly plenary session, sparking controversy over the prosecution's supplementary investigation authority.
The criminal justice system is undergoing significant changes with enhanced protection for crime victims and expanded grounds for dismissal of public prosecution.
Public concerns are mounting over what many view as hasty and contradictory amendments.
editorial.bodyTr: An amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act has been submitted to the National Assembly plenary session, sparking controversy over the non-grant of supplementary investigation rights to the prosecution. With changes to the criminal justice system, including victim protection and expanded grounds for dismissal of charges, public concerns are mounting.

editorial.titleTr: Editorial: Aren't We Afraid of the Fallout from Abolishing Supplementary Investigations?
summaryTr: The Democratic Party forcibly passed the abolition of the prosecution's supplementary investigative authority.
The foundation of the judicial system is being shaken, with growing concerns about infringement on victims' rights.
Concerns are mounting over procedural issues and adverse effects in investigative operations.
editorial.bodyTr: The Democratic Party's forced passage of a criminal procedure law revision that abolishes the prosecution's supplementary investigative authority is shaking the foundation of the judicial system. This poses a significant risk of infringing upon the rights of crime victims and socially disadvantaged groups, while raising constitutional questions regarding equal rights and investigative authority. Concerns are growing over procedural issues that emerged in the hasty legislative push as well as potential adverse effects that may arise in actual investigative operations going forward.

summaryTr: A special inspector position tasked with investigating the president's relatives has remained vacant for a decade.
As both ruling and opposition parties began nominating candidates, discussions on normalizing the system gained momentum.
To fulfill the original purpose of monitoring power, partisan considerations must be set aside and an uncomfortable figure appointed.
editorials.bodyTr: The Special Prosecutor position, tasked with investigating the president's relatives and senior government officials, has remained vacant for a decade, and now both ruling and opposition parties are moving to nominate candidates. The article emphasizes that to fulfill the original purpose of the system—monitoring power—a decisive choice is needed to appoint someone most inconvenient to those in power, setting aside partisan interests.

editorials.titleTr: Editorial: Military's Shocking Lapses—From Empty Gun Alert to Missing Operation Reports
summaryTr: U.S. military drone mistaken for North Korean aircraft and shot down attempt in front-line Paju.
Military operational system incompetence exposed due to missed notification of training report.
Urgent need to tighten discipline in front-line units and improve response systems.
editorials.bodyTr: A recent incident in which South Korean forces at the frontline in Paju, Gyeonggi Province mistakenly attempted to shoot down a U.S. military drone, believing it to be a North Korean aircraft, has raised serious concerns. The incident, stemming from the omission of a training notification report, reveals systemic incompetence in the military's operational and response systems as well as a broader discipline problem among frontline units.

editorial.titleTr: Opinion: More Dismissals Won't Keep Anyone from Questioning the President's Trial
summaryTr: The Democratic Party has proposed an amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act that would add grounds for dismissal of charges.
The opposition criticizes it as 'tailor-made legislation' designed to eliminate the president's legal risks.
Expanding grounds for charge dismissal while securing the power to appoint Supreme Court justices undermines judicial independence.
editorial.bodyTr: The Democratic Party submitted an amendment to the Criminal Procedure Act to the National Assembly plenary session, adding grounds for dismissal of public prosecution by courts in addition to abolishing prosecutors' supplementary investigation authority. It is problematic not only that the party is pushing forward with the abolition of supplementary investigation authority despite concerns that socially vulnerable groups will suffer harm, but also that the amendment to Article 327 of the Criminal Procedure Act on dismissal of public prosecution, quietly inserted into the bill, cannot be overlooked. The Democratic Party claims it merely codifies Supreme Court precedents, but the opposition and legal community point out that this is "tailor-made legislation" aimed at legitimately removing President Lee Jae-myung's judicial risks. There is reason for such criticism. The ruling party has previously attempted to introduce a special prosecutor and cancel indictments regarding cases involving the president, claiming they were manipulated prosecutions. However, they faced public backlash, confirmed by the party's defeat in the Seoul mayoral election and other local elections. This time, the Democratic Party added two grounds for dismissal of public prosecution: when indictment was raised through serious illegal investigation, and when indictment was raised in manifest deviation of prosecutorial discretion. This differs from current law, which specifies only six procedural defects, such as when the indictment procedure is invalid due to legal violation. The inclusion of subjective expressions like "serious" and "manifest" opens the door for courts to make arbitrary decisions on politically sensitive cases, a criticism that is difficult to avoid. Moreover, while indictment cancellation is possible only before a first trial verdict is announced, dismissal of public prosecution can be decided by courts even in second and third trials, making all cases involving the president potential targets. The Democratic Party has already passed legislation to increase the number of Supreme Court justices. Chief Justice Jo Hee-dae's term ends next June. The president plans to appoint 22 Supreme Court justices, including a new chief justice, during his tenure. This amounts to the president himself filling the composition of the Supreme Court that will make the final judgment on trials involving him. If expanded grounds for dismissal of public prosecution are added to this, it becomes theoretically possible for Supreme Court justices appointed by the president to rule on dismissal of public prosecution in cases involving the president. Being perceived as using changes in law and institutions as a shield for those in power would be a stain on the president's legacy. If the Democratic Party's claim that this legislation is not for a specific individual is true, it should stop the forced passage. Yet neither the president nor anyone at the Blue House has said anything. Should the amendment pass the National Assembly, it is hoped that the president will exercise his veto power to independently protect the judicial branch's independence and resolve public distrust. That is the path to securing the legitimacy of state governance.

editorial.title: Demographic threshold
editorial.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population. 한국이 하루아침에 늙어버린 것은 아니다. 하지만 모든 사회는 인구통계 전망이 미래를 설명하는 것에서 현재를 설명하는 것으로 바뀌는 지점에 도달하게 된다. 그 순간이 이번 주에 도래했다. 지난 화요일 통계청이 발표한 2025년 공식 인구조사 데이터에 따르면, 65세 이상 인구가 전체 인구의 20.7%를 차지하면서 한국이 공식적으로 세계의 초고령사회에 진입했다. 동시에 생산가능인구는 69.2%로 하락해 비교 가능한 통계가 시작된 2015년 이후 처음으로 70% 선 아래로 내려갔다. 이 수치들은 자의적인 기준선을 넘어서는 것보다 더욱 중대한 무언가를 확인시켜준다는 점에서 의미가 있다. 한국은 더 이상 인구 구조의 전환을 앞두고 있는 것이 아니라 이미 그 전환을 완료한 것이다. 따라서 이제 과제는 인구 구조를 복원하는 방법이 아니라 생산성과 사회적 결속을 희생하지 않으면서 영구적으로 고령화되고 성장이 둔화된 사회를 관리하는 방법이다.

노동정책은 왜 과거의 논쟁들이 더 이상 현재의 현실에 맞지 않는지를 잘 보여준다. 의무 정년을 60세 이상으로 연장해야 한다는 주장은 실제 문제를 반영한다. 많은 노동자들이 국민연금 수급 자격을 갖추기 수년 전에 직장을 떠나기 때문이다. 한편 기업들은 한국의 연공급 체계 하에서 근로자를 계속 고용하면 노동비용이 급증하면서 신규 채용을 억제할 것이라고 주장한다. 하지만 이 문제를 고령 노동자와 젊은 구직자 간의 경쟁으로 보는 것은 증상을 원인으로 착각하는 것이다. 더 근본적인 제약은 근속연수를 생산성보다 더 많이 보상하는 임금체계다. 임금제도를 개혁하지 않으면 정년 연장은 채용 유인을 약화시키고 경쟁력도 함께 떨어뜨릴 수 있다. 보다 유연한 정년 이후 재고용 정책과 함께 직무 기반 및 성과 기반 급여로의 점진적 전환이 더 지속 가능한 타협책을 제시할 것이다.

같은 논리가 연금과 복지에도 적용된다. 한국의 노년부양비는 29.9로 상승했으며, 이는 대략 3.3명의 생산가능인구가 한 명의 노인을 부양한다는 의미다. 고령화지수가 200을 넘어서면서 모든 어린이 한 명마다 두 명 이상의 노인이 있다. 연금, 의료비, 장기요양비에 대한 공공지출은 필연적으로 증가할 것이고, 한편 세수 기반은 더 느리게 확대될 것이다. 근로자 기여율 인상이나 급여 수정 같은 점진적 조정들은 재정 부담을 미룰 수 있지만 근본적인 불균형을 해결할 수는 없다. 한국은 결국 국민연금, 기초연금, 직역연금 체계를 더 잘 통합하고 선거 일정이 아닌 인구통계 변화에 대응하는 자동조정 메커니즘을 필요로 한다.

이민과 지역 발전도 같은 장기적 관점을 요구한다. 외국인 주민이 한국 인구의 4.1%를 차지하고 있으며, 이 중 89.3%가 생산가능연령대다. 그들의 제조업, 농업, 돌봄 서비스에 대한 기여도는 이미 상당하다. 하지만 임시 노동 프로그램은 축소되는 국내 노동력을 대체할 수 없다. 한국은 영구 정착을 원하는 고숙련 전문가들을 더 적극적으로 유치하기 위해 경쟁해야 한다. 또 다른 중요한 문제는 서울 수도권에 인구의 50.9%가 집중되어 있다는 점으로, 이는 주택 압박을 심화시키면서 동시에 지역 경제를 공동화시키고 있다. 더 강한 지역 산업 기반이 중앙정부의 더 많은 이전 지출보다 더 중요해질 것이다.

경제 적응은 노동시장을 넘어선다. 서울 가구의 40% 이상이 이제 한 사람으로 구성되어 있으며, 더 큰 가족을 위해 설계된 주택 모델들은 점차 구식이 되고 있다. 시장과 정책결정자 모두 소비 패턴, 주택 수요, 노인 돌봄의 변화에 맞춰 조정해야 하며, 인공지능과 다른 생산성 향상 기술에 대한 투자는 축소되는 노동력을 보완하는 데 도움을 줄 것이다.

인구통계 기준선들은 종종 이정표로 묘사된다. 실제로는 제도들이 자신들이 봉사하기 위해 건설된 사회를 따라가지 못하기 시작하는 지점을 표시한다. 한국은 임시방편이 아닌 훨씬 더 구조적인 적응을 요구하는 시대에 진입했다. 한국이 번영하고 응집력 있는 사회로 남을지 여부는 그 노동시장, 연금 체계, 그리고 광범위한 경제 구조가 변화하는 인구와 얼마나 성공적으로 함께 진화하는지에 달려 있다.

editorials.title: Demographic threshold
editorials.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population. Retail investors took losses while foreign investors reaped gains.
Extreme volatility exposed structural vulnerabilities in the Korean stock market.
editorial.bodyTr: The stock market, which had sent investors into a panic with record-breaking plunges, staged a sharp rebound. The Kospi, which had been marching toward all-time highs since the beginning of this year, has undergone sharp corrections since July.

editorials.titleTr: President Faces Growing Legal Conflict Over Nolle Prosequi Dismissal, Must Exercise Veto Power
summaryTr: The Democratic Party passed an amendment to abolish the prosecution's supplementary investigation authority through the National Assembly.
Crime victims, women's groups, and the legal community strongly opposed it on grounds of unconstitutionality.
A majority of the public also wants to maintain the supplementary investigation authority.
editorials.bodyTr: A criminal procedure law amendment bill eliminating prosecutorial supplementary investigative authority passed the National Assembly on the 31st, led by the Democratic Party. Once this law is confirmed at the State Council meeting, prosecutors will lose all forms of direct investigative authority. Over the past month, crime victims, women's organizations, academics, and legal professionals have opposed the amendment, citing concerns about legal unconstitutionality and public safety risks. Various opinion polls have shown that a majority of the public wishes to retain prosecutorial supplementary investigative authority.
